bp: Construction projects create a constant need to say exactly what information one party must deliver to another: which building objects, properties, formats, and checks are required before design, construction, or handover can proceed. Standards such as Industry Foundation Classes and Information Delivery Specification exist so those requirements can be exchanged by software rather than retyped or interpreted from prose. The practical problem is that the standard form is XML, a rigid tree of tags and values that asks users to know abstract entity names and formal schema rules. Many of the people who know the project requirement are not XML specialists or standards experts. This paper serves the gap between human intent and machine-readable exchange. Its object is not a general chat answer, but a translation from ordinary requirement language into valid IDS XML, so global construction workflows can share requirements without forcing every participant to become a standards technician.
wh: The hard part is that natural language and standards documents organize meaning in opposite ways. A person may say, in ordinary words, that a wall must contain a fire rating, a material classification, or some other required property. The IDS format needs that intent placed into exact XML locations with the right entity definitions and allowed structure. If one tag is missing, one concept is mapped to the wrong abstract entity, or one condition is written in a form the schema rejects, the output may look technical while being unusable. Existing tools can still require the user to understand the standard well enough to guide the tool. That defeats the purpose, because the bottleneck is not only typing XML; it is knowing how a building requirement should be normalized into the standard's formal vocabulary. The central tension is therefore flexibility versus validity: the input should be human-friendly, but the output must obey a strict industrial format.
naive: A smart beginner would first build a form or template library: ask users to fill fields, choose building elements from menus, and then paste those fields into a fixed XML skeleton. That works for repeated simple cases, but construction requirements vary in wording, scope, and implied constraints. A template can miss requirements that do not fit its slots, while too many slots recreate the same high learning curve as the standard itself. Another beginner approach is to ask a language model to write XML directly. That may produce plausible tags, but plausible is not the same as valid. Without grounding in the IDS schema, the model can invent structures, misplace requirements, or smooth over details that software exchange depends on.
ap: The paper's central move is to place a language model inside a schema-grounded structuring process. The user writes industry information requirements in natural language. The system uses the model's ability to interpret meaning across varied wording, but it does not treat free text generation as enough. It normalizes the requirement into the Information Delivery Specification's expected XML form, using the schema as the boundary that defines what a valid answer can look like. In concrete terms, SGSS tries to make the model act like a translator with a rulebook open: understand the human sentence, identify the construction information being requested, map that meaning to standard concepts, and produce XML that a standards-aware tool can accept. The paper is presented as a demonstration, so the emphasis is on making industrial exchange more accessible rather than introducing a benchmark-centered prediction task.
mech: The mechanism begins with a user-supplied requirement stated in ordinary construction language. That text carries intent: what information must be delivered, for which building or project objects, and under what specification-like conditions. SGSS then asks a large language model to interpret the semantic content, meaning the model must move past surface wording and infer the role each phrase plays in the requested exchange. The next transformation is normalization. Instead of leaving the requirement as prose, the system aligns it with the concepts expected by Industry Foundation Classes and Information Delivery Specification. The schema-grounding step matters here: it constrains the possible output to the formal XML shape accepted by IDS, including the right kinds of nested elements and entity references. The system then emits IDS XML as the product, not as an explanation. A downstream construction information exchange process can use that XML to check or request data automatically. The abstract does not disclose all internal stages, such as whether SGSS uses retrieval over schema documentation, validation after generation, repair loops, or fixed prompts. What it does support is the pipeline shape: natural-language requirement goes in; semantic interpretation and schema-based normalization occur; valid IDS XML comes out.
math: The mathematical idea underneath is structured translation under constraints. Translation here does not mean changing English to another human language; it means changing a flexible sentence into a formal tree. XML is a tree because each piece sits inside a parent piece, and software reads meaning partly from that nesting. The system must decide which parts of the sentence correspond to which branches and leaves of the tree. A second idea is constrained generation: among many possible strings the model could produce, only some obey the IDS schema. The schema acts like a set of allowed moves, similar to rules that say which pieces may follow which other pieces in a legal document. A third idea is semantic matching, the act of deciding that two differently worded descriptions refer to the same standard concept. The tradeoff is freedom versus exactness. Natural language gives users freedom to express requirements as they think about them, while XML gives machines exactness. SGSS is useful only if the model's learned language patterns can be narrowed by schema rules enough to preserve both. The abstract also invokes learning from language-model semantic understanding, but it does not specify training data, scoring functions, or validation math, so those details cannot be assumed.
dots: This paper sits with the conference's language-model papers that treat fluent text as only one component inside a controlled system. It is close to tool-use and agent work because the model is being asked to take an action with consequences: produce a formal artifact that another system will read, not merely answer a question. It also connects to information and learning themes. The input requirement contains useful information in a loose human form; the output preserves that information in a stricter machine form, discarding ambiguity where the schema requires a decision. Compared with retrieval or ranking papers, the sorting problem is not a list of documents or products but a list of possible standard entities and XML structures. Compared with knowledge-graph and semantic-web work, the common pressure is respecting formal relationships rather than flattening everything into prose. The neighboring idea is grounded language modeling: a model becomes more useful when its flexible interpretation is tied to an external structure that can reject invalid shape.
ww: The approach should improve over the naive alternatives because it separates two jobs that are often confused. Humans are good at knowing the practical requirement: what information a designer, contractor, owner, or downstream tool needs. Standards are good at giving that requirement a stable machine-readable form. The failure happens when humans must manually bridge those two worlds. SGSS lets the model handle the language bridge while the schema keeps the bridge from drifting into unsupported XML. This is stronger than a fixed form because the model can handle varied phrasing and requirements that do not fit one template exactly. It is stronger than unrestricted model output because the target is not merely a convincing-looking answer; it is normalized IDS XML. The method fits the domain because construction information exchange is already standardized, so there is an external structure to ground against. The model is not inventing the destination language from scratch. It is using human wording to choose and fill pieces of a known formal format.
po: The payoff is accessibility. People who understand construction requirements can express them in natural language and receive IDS XML without first mastering the XML syntax, abstract entity definitions, and standards-specific tool behavior. That can lower the learning curve around Industry Foundation Classes and Information Delivery Specification and make automated information exchange easier to adopt across international construction workflows. The abstract frames SGSS as a demonstration, so the result is a usable bridge between human-friendly input and structured standards rather than a claim about a new theoretical limit. If the generated XML is valid and faithful, project teams gain a faster path from requirement writing to software-checkable exchange.
limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. SGSS must correctly understand the user's requirement, and the requirement itself must contain enough detail to map into IDS XML. If the prose is ambiguous, incomplete, or uses local construction terminology that the model misreads, schema grounding may produce valid XML with the wrong meaning. The system also depends on accurate knowledge of Industry Foundation Classes and IDS schema rules. The abstract does not report datasets, error rates, validation procedure, repair strategy, or user studies, so it does not prove reliability across all project types, languages, standards versions, or adversarial inputs. Valid XML is necessary, but not sufficient, for faithful information exchange.
